analysis.one_liner: Removes the public-interest review for natural gas exports and hands regulators sole approval power over LNG terminals.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill 27-21 and the Rules Committee twice prepared it for floor debate, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the requirement that exporting natural gas serve the "public interest," a test that currently lets the government weigh how exports affect American energy prices and supply [S2][S4]. It would also strip out restrictions tied to free trade agreements and make the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission the only agency that can approve or deny LNG export and import terminals — and it would require that regulator to treat any export as automatically consistent with the public interest [S2][S3][S4]. The bill cleared committee and was prepped for a floor debate, but the House never voted on it [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas producers and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal developers gain the most. Today, exports must pass a public-interest review that can consider effects on domestic energy prices and supply; the bill would remove that test entirely and bar other agencies from blocking terminals, making approvals faster and near-automatic [S2][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gas producers and LNG terminal developers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Natural Gas Act requirement that FERC authorize natural gas exports only if they are in the public interest, along with restrictions related to free trade agreements [S2].

Gives FERC exclusive authority to approve or deny LNG export and import terminal applications, and requires FERC to deem any export or import 'consistent with the public interest,' removing its discretion to weigh harm to domestic consumers [S2][S4].
Preserves presidential authority to block exports to sanctioned countries or state sponsors of terrorism, but leaves no general public-interest check [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Households and businesses that buy natural gas could pay more: large-scale exports pull domestic supply toward foreign buyers, and the bill removes the public-interest review that currently weighs that effect [S2][S4]. Communities near proposed LNG terminals would lose one layer of federal review over siting and construction [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas consumers and communities near terminals

drawbacks.text: The bill would require regulators to treat every export application as automatically in the public interest, eliminating the government's ability to consider whether shipping gas overseas raises prices or tightens supply for American homes and factories [S2][S4].

Making FERC the exclusive approver of LNG terminals, while stripping the older public-interest and free-trade-agreement provisions, reduces the checks on where and how export facilities are built [S2][S3].

Supporters would argue faster export approvals strengthen allies and energy jobs; the honest cost is that those gains come without any weighing of effects on domestic energy bills, since the weighing mechanism is what the bill deletes [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow mainly to gas exporters in the form of faster, near-automatic approvals. The costs fall diffusely on gas customers, who lose the public-interest review that can account for what heavy exporting does to domestic prices, and on communities near terminals facing less federal scrutiny. The bill removes a consumer safeguard without replacing it with anything.

outcome.mechanism: The bill passed committee 27-21 and was placed on the House calendar, and the Rules Committee twice set up floor debate, but the House never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 21, 2023 and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S6].
A subcommittee forwarded it 16-9 on February 28, and the full committee ordered it reported 27-21 on March 9; it was reported amended on March 23 and placed on the Union Calendar [S6].
The Rules Committee reported two resolutions, in September 2023, providing for structured floor debate on the bill, but no House vote ever occurred [S6].
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill died on the calendar [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic natural gas customers came out ahead: the public-interest review on exports and the free-trade-agreement restrictions remain in force because the bill never became law. Gas producers gained nothing, but lost nothing they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Domestic gas customers; exporters gained nothing

for.name: 7 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all seven were added around its March 23 committee report.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Voted 27-21 to order the bill reported, amended, on March 9, 2023, and reported it March 23.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported two resolutions providing for structured House debate of the bill, in September 2023.

against.name: 9 and 21 committee members
against.role: Minority of the Energy and Commerce subcommittee and full committee
against.what_they_did: Voted against the bill at subcommittee (16-9) and full committee (27-21) markups.

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Republicans and the committee votes were close and narrow — 16-9 in subcommittee and 27-21 in full committee — with no Democratic cosponsors listed [S5][S6].

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and LNG terminal developers
industries.note: The bill would remove the public-interest test on exports and make terminal approvals near-automatic under FERC, speeding permits and locking in a larger export industry. Its gain comes at the potential expense of domestic gas prices and local review of terminal siting [S2][S4].

industries.industry: Utilities, manufacturers, and other large natural gas buyers
industries.note: Unrestricted exports tend to pull domestic supply toward foreign markets, which can raise the price these buyers — and the households they serve — pay for gas [S2][S4].
